title: Review decks: how topics change, and the look

steps.page: How a topic changes over rounds
steps.intro: Judge here: which way should a deck treat a topic over time? You said you wanted real cases first. Each drawing shows the same three: voice input (answered once), the pencil (answered, then reopened by you), and "what came before" (built and rejected twice). Press a picture to open it at full size.

steps.path: Any deck, from its first round to the finished build
steps.headline: What should happen to a topic after you answer it?
steps.today: Each round is a separate deck. Earlier rounds sit behind a History button, which you dislike.
steps.checked: Opened the round-9 deck today; the History button is still in its header.
steps.problem: You have not decided. You described two ideas: a question that evolves into refined versions, or an answered question that sinks to the bottom with its round.
steps.proposal: Pick one, and say what to borrow from another. All three keep one link per feature and the four stages across the top.

options.label: In place
pros: A topic never moves, so you can find it again.
An open topic shows its whole story above the question.
cons: The longest page; it grows every round.
Open topics sit scattered among settled ones.

options.label: Answered sinks
pros: The page opens on exactly what needs you.
A reopened topic returns to the top and says where it came from.
cons: An open topic shows one line of its past, not the full story, unless I add that.

options.label: Versions
pros: A question truly evolves in one spot.
Short page, fixed places.
cons: Earlier versions hide behind arrows; you could answer without seeing them.
A new control to learn, and the most work to build.

steps.path: An open topic that has been through several rounds
steps.headline: How much of a topic's past should show without pressing anything?
steps.today: In drawing A the full story shows. In B one summary line shows. In C none shows until you step back.
steps.checked: Compared the three drawings on this page today.
steps.problem: You disliked both a hidden History button and a busy page. This is the trade between them.
steps.proposal: Pick how much is visible on an open topic. It applies to whichever shape you chose above.

options.label: One summary line, the rest opens on request
pros: Calm page.
The past is one press away, on the topic itself.
cons: One press to read your own earlier words.

options.label: The full story, always
pros: Nothing hidden.
cons: A topic argued over five rounds puts ten lines above its question.

options.label: Nothing unless asked
pros: Shortest page.
cons: Close to the History button you disliked.

steps.page: Marking a row as looked at
steps.intro: Judge here: how should you tell a deck you have looked at a row? You said you do not want a row "accidentally taken as approved just because i didnt read or see it". Four drawings of the same five rows, half finished.

steps.headline: How should a row be marked as looked at?
steps.today: A row has one pencil. A row you leave alone counts as approved.
steps.problem: A row you never reached is approved the same as one you read and liked.
steps.proposal: Pick one. The comment box at the foot of the page, which you like, stays in all four.

options.label: Tick or change
pros: "Not looked at" and "fine" can never be confused.
The page counts what is left.
cons: One press per row; slow on a long list.

options.label: Seen as you scroll
pros: No extra buttons.
Next tells you if you skipped rows.
cons: "Seen" means it was on screen, not that you read it.
Scroll tracking can misfire on a phone.

options.label: Approve the rest
pros: Fast when most rows are fine.
The button wakes only after the last row has been on screen.
cons: One press still approves rows you scrolled past unread.

options.label: As today
pros: Nothing to learn.

steps.path: Finishing a page with rows not looked at
steps.headline: Should rows you have not looked at stop you sending the deck?
steps.today: Nothing stops you. Untouched rows are sent as approved.
steps.problem: A warning can be ignored; a block can be annoying when you only care about two rows.

options.label: Warn, list them, let me send anyway
pros: You stay in charge.
Rows you skipped are sent as "not looked at", never as approved.
cons: I may build on rows you never read; they come back next round marked so.

options.label: Block until every row is handled
pros: Nothing unread is ever built on.
cons: A long list must be finished before any answer reaches me.

steps.intro: Judge here: is this the right look? The seven drawings on the earlier pages are in your Ivory Schematic colours, with dots and plain words where last round had outlined labels.

steps.headline: Do these drawings look like part of YouCoded?
steps.today: Last round you called the drawing ugly and said you hated its "fingernail styling".
steps.checked: Read your round-9 comment on question E-1 today.
steps.problem: I took "fingernail" to mean the small rounded outlined labels. If I guessed wrong, the new drawings miss the point.
steps.proposal: Yes means I build decks to look like these. No or Other: say what is still off, or drag across the part of the picture you mean.
steps.caption: Drawing B from the first page.

steps.headline: What was the "fingernail styling"?
steps.today: I removed every small rounded outlined label and replaced each with a dot and a plain word.
steps.checked: Compared last round's drawing with this round's today.
steps.problem: I am guessing at your meaning.
steps.proposal: Pick the closest, or write it.
steps.caption: Last round's drawing, the one you disliked.

options.label: The small rounded outlined labels
pros: Already gone in the new drawings.

options.label: The row of stage buttons at the top
pros: Now the app's own tab strip.

options.label: Something else (please write it)
pros: I fix the right thing.

steps.headline: Should decks use your theme's typeface too?
steps.today: Decks now open in your theme's colours. The lettering is still the deck's own typewriter-style face.
steps.checked: Opened a deck in Ivory Schematic today.
steps.problem: The app uses your theme's typeface (Space Grotesk). The deck does not, so it still reads as a different product.
steps.proposal: Yes makes each deck fetch the typeface from Google when it opens, as the app does. No keeps the current lettering.

calls.call: The four safety checks are back, on unless you switch them off.
